Does the answer depend on the pooling method?

With two or three studies the Cochrane Handbook (10.10.4.4–10.10.4.5) asks for a sensitivity analysis comparing interval methods rather than a choice between them. Both are given here; the published interval is the first row.

Table 8. Does the answer depend on the pooling method?
IntervalMethodSummary (95% CI)
as publishedREML0.6561 (0.484 to 0.8894)
sensitivity (Handbook 10.10.4.5)REML with Hartung-Knapp, t on k-1 = 1 degree(s) of freedom (t = 12.7062)0.6561 (0.0913 to 4.7135)

The published point is 0.6561 and the house-rule point is 0.6561. The number a reader remembers does not move; what differs is the precision claim. That is why nothing downstream catches this -- every memorable quantity survives.

A floor of 1 is applied to the variance-inflation factor so the adjustment can never narrow an interval below the unadjusted one. That guard is the recognised modification for exactly this instability, and its existence is evidence the small-k behaviour is a known problem with known handling rather than a novel judgement.

  1. No GRADE assessment or reconciliation record is held in this object, so the certainty of this evidence has not been rated. This is recorded as a declared departure under Cochrane Handbook §III.3.4.1: the review reports a pooled estimate for which no certainty assessment was made. Rating it here would require two assessors and an adjudicator, and a rating produced by neither is not a GRADE assessment whatever letter it carries.
  2. Read this beside `whether the estimand was established`. That flag records that every contributing trial measures the same quantity. It records nothing about what that quantity was measured against -- whether the comparators are of one kind, whether each comparison was randomised, whether it was concurrent. The two questions were never separated. Named as P48 in PAGE-STANDARD.md v1.21.0 and swept by scripts/audit_mixed_contrast_pools.py.

It has now been checked. JUPITER registers a FIVE-component composite: 'Time to Major Cardiac Event (Cardiovascular Death, Stroke, Myocardial Infarction, Hospitalization Due to Unstable Angina or Arterial Revascularization)'. HOPE-3 registers two co-primaries, 'The composite of; Cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke.' and 'The composite of; cardiovascular death, resuscitated cardiac arrest, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, heart failure, arterial revascularizations'. Neither is JUPITER's. JUPITER counts any stroke and any myocardial infarction where both HOPE-3 composites count non-fatal only; JUPITER counts hospitalisation for unstable angina and neither HOPE-3 composite does; HOPE-3's second adds resuscitated cardiac arrest and heart failure, which JUPITER's does not. Why it is referred rather than withdrawn hereWithdrawing a published estimate is a published-number decision and this pass was scoped to establish the estimand, not to take that decision. The finding is complete and stated; the decision is Mahmood's.
Scopevenous thromboembolism -- deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism -- one outcome harmonised across both trials
ScopeNot established -- the abstract was read, the outcome list was not
The finding of this comparisonThe only published synthesis of these two trials avoided the estimand problem this pool has. Joseph et al. pooled individual participant data on one outcome defined identically in both trials. This object pools each trial's own registered primary, and those differ -- which this object's question already states. The comparison therefore does not adjudicate our number; it shows that the literature, given the same two trials, chose a different and more defensible target. Whether to re-pool on a harmonised outcome is a content decision and is not made here.
Population label WITHDRAWNThis object described its population as 'adults with stroke'. That is wrong and it is WITHDRAWN. Both contributing trials are primary prevention in people without established cardiovascular disease. Read from ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 on 2026-08-21: NCT00239681 is JUPITER, registered under the single condition 'Elevated high-sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hsCRP)'; NCT00468923 is HOPE-3, an intermediate-risk primary-prevention trial. And the origin of the error is identifiable: hope-3's registry `conditions` array reads Cardiovascular Disease and Stroke because stroke is an outcome it counts, not because its participants had one. A conditions field lists what a trial is about, which is not the same as what its participants have, and reading it as a population label turns an endpoint into a diagnosis. The correct description is: adults without established cardiovascular disease, at elevated risk. No estimate changes.

Paper

Each statement below cites the record it came from; those sources are listed at the end of every section. Where the record holds nothing, the section says so by name rather than being left out, so a procedure that was not carried out can be told from one that simply was never mentioned.

Title

Rosuvastatin in adults with stroke1

This object described its population as 'adults with stroke'. That is wrong and it is withdrawn. Both contributing trials are primary prevention in people without established cardiovascular disease. Read from ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 on 2026-08-21: NCT00239681 is JUPITER, registered under the single condition 'Elevated high-sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hsCRP)'; NCT00468923 is HOPE-3, an intermediate-risk primary-prevention trial. And the origin of the error is identifiable: hope-3's registry `conditions` array reads Cardiovascular Disease and Stroke because stroke is an outcome it counts, not because its participants had one. A conditions field lists what a trial is about, which is not the same as what its participants have, and reading it as a population label turns an endpoint into a diagnosis. The correct description is: adults without established cardiovascular disease, at elevated risk. No estimate changes.2

Introduction

Background. This review asks: In adults with stroke, does Rosuvastatin compared with placebo affect the outcome each trial registered as its primary, which differ across the 2 trials here? It pools 2 randomised trials. The outcome pooled is Time to Major Cardiac Event (Cardiovascular Death, Stroke, Myocardial Infarction, Hospitalization Due to Unstable Angina.1

Results

The pooled odds ratio for time to Major Cardiac Event (Cardiovascular Death, Stroke, Myocardial Infarction, Hospitalization Due to Unstable Angina was 0.656 (0.484 to 0.889) across 2 trials.1

This pool is referred, not withdrawn. The pooled odds ratio 0.6561 (0.484 to 0.8894) averages JUPITER's five-component composite with one of HOPE-3's two co-primaries, and the object cannot say which. This is the estimand-mixing shape that caused sglt2-hf's k=4 pool to be withdrawn.2

The trials' results were poorly consistent with one another: I-squared, the share of the variation between them that is more than chance alone would produce, was 80.2%; the estimated variance of the true effects between trials (tau-squared) was 0.0387, the heterogeneity test statistic Q was 5.04, on degrees of freedom 1.3

The grounds for pooling are recorded as: The extractor recovered a pooled result from this page, so the page pooled these trials. Whether they should have been pooled is not established by conversion - several pages in this corpus pooled harm with efficacy, or distinct agents, and their estimates were withdrawn for that reason. Where a later pool on this page rests on the same grounds, they are not restated.4

The full model output for every pooled outcome -- the call, the estimator, the heterogeneity statistics and the back-transformed interval -- is reproduced verbatim as Extended data at the end of this article, so every number above can be checked against the software that produced it.5

Limitations

What this review does not give a clinician: the number of events in each arm, any absolute effect or number needed to treat and any measure of harm. A relative effect cannot be turned into the benefit or the risk facing one patient without them, so this review can support a judgement about what these trials found and not a judgement about what to do.1
